about: The same five synthetic test viewers as v0.1, shown v0.2 (two contact sheets of stills and the narration, through OpenRouter). Not people and not a review signature. Em dashes in their answers are replaced by commas.

viewers.who: a Scrum Master in a 300-person company that adopted a scaled Agile framework two years ago; you feel the ceremonies have grown and the values have faded. Sceptical of buzzwords.

answer.why_stop: Seeing the Agile Manifesto quoted on an oversized yellow note caught my eye because my daily existence is suffering through scaled Agile theatre.
answer.why_drop: You quote 'individuals and interactions over processes and tools', and two scenes later you pitch a 50-role org chart and markdown files for a single task. It's automated corporate bureaucracy pretending to be agile.
answer.story_back: The pitch claims you can fix scaled Agile by spinning up and shutting down temporary mini-companies made of text files, humans, and AI agents for every individual task.
confusing: How creating a 50-node hierarchy for one task doesn't collapse under its own coordination tax.
Whether 'agents' means LLM bots or offshore contractors.
How replacing team trust with 'files anyone can read' honors individuals over processes.
answer.best_moment: Scene 2, simply reminding everyone that the 2001 manifesto was four lines about human interactions, before frameworks ruined it.
answer.one_change: Stop dressing up automated agent orchestration in Agile Manifesto nostalgia; just explain how the AI agent pipeline actually ships code without infinite overhead.
answer.weakest_moment: Scene 4 proudly scaling up to a 50-role hierarchy for a single deliverable. That is a project manager's fever dream.
answer.what_i_would_do_tomorrow: Close the app and complain in our Slack backchannel about consultants repackaging micro-management as AI innovation.

viewers.who: a founder of a 6-person startup who uses AI coding agents daily and wonders how to organise more of them. Impatient; scrolls fast on LinkedIn.

answer.why_stop: The opening promise is relevant: spin up a temporary company of agents for one task. The visual metaphor is immediately understandable.
answer.why_drop: Scene 3 turns into a long definition with near-identical diagrams and no concrete example of the cell actually producing something.
answer.story_back: Agile Cells are temporary, file-defined teams of humans and AI agents assembled for one job and shut down when it is finished.
confusing: It is unclear which roles are humans and which are agents.
The jump from the Agile Manifesto to agent cells is asserted rather than explained.
Fifty roles looks like an org-chart gimmick, not a useful operating model.
The film says files define the rules but never shows what those files contain.
answer.best_moment: The opening animation where a large organisation collapses into a small temporary cell, paired with 'When the task is done, we close it.'
answer.one_change: Replace the middle diagrams with one concrete before-and-after example showing a cell completing a real deliverable, including the actual human and agent roles.
answer.weakest_moment: The repeated 10, 20, 50 role diagrams, which feel like filler and make the concept seem needlessly bureaucratic.
answer.what_i_would_do_tomorrow: Save it and click through to the underlying framework, but I would not share it yet because the film does not prove the model works.

viewers.who: a CTO at a mid-sized firm who buys outsourced work (websites, CRM set-up, social media). You want to know what you could actually buy and whether it is real.

answer.why_stop: The claim of spinning up and tearing down a full company for a single task caught my eye.
answer.why_drop: Lecturing me on the 2001 Agile Manifesto immediately feels like academic consultant fluff rather than a real product.
answer.story_back: They use temporary, file-defined swarms of AI agents and humans to execute discrete outsource deliverables like websites or CRMs.
confusing: Ratio of real humans to automated agents doing the work
How 50 roles for one task doesn't create massive latency and cost overhead
Whether this is a service agency or software I have to run myself
answer.best_moment: Scene 5 showing the real architecture and named roles used to produce the film.
answer.one_change: Delete the Agile history lesson and show a live CRM or website being deployed by this system.
answer.weakest_moment: Scene 2 showing the Agile Manifesto text on a giant sticky note.
answer.what_i_would_do_tomorrow: Keep scrolling; smells like theoretical framework vaporware without proof of delivery.

viewers.who: a developer who has done Agile since 2005, read the Manifesto many times, and dislikes people misquoting it.

answer.why_stop: The opening image is visually distinctive and the promise of a temporary company for one task is a credible hook.
answer.why_drop: After the accurate Manifesto reference, the film repeats glowing org charts and role counts without showing how a cell actually works or solves a real problem.
answer.story_back: Agile Cells are temporary, file-defined teams of people and agents assembled to complete one task and then disbanded.
confusing: What makes this Agile rather than merely a temporary project team or agency?
How do people and agents interact in practice?
What does 'scale' mean here: more roles, more cells, or larger work?
Why are the cell's rules and files sufficient for accountability and coordination?
The film says 'a small team' and then shows up to 50 roles without explaining the boundary.
answer.best_moment: The manifesto card stating 'Individuals and interactions over processes and tools' gives the concept a clear principle to test against.
answer.one_change: Replace most of the org-chart montage with a concrete before-and-after workflow showing a cell forming, collaborating, delivering one task, and being dismantled.
answer.weakest_moment: The 10, 20, and 50 role sequence is repetitive exposition disguised as escalation.
answer.what_i_would_do_tomorrow: I would look for the actual cell files, operating rules, and a concrete example showing one completing a task.

viewers.who: someone who does not work in software, scrolling Instagram Reels in the evening, watching with sound off.

answer.why_stop: The glowing neon constellation blob against the dark background looked like some cool sci-fi aesthetic for half a second.
answer.why_drop: A giant yellow document appeared on screen lecturing me about corporate manifesto values from 2001. I'm on Instagram to relax, not attend mandatory tech company onboarding.
answer.story_back: It is trying to pitch a corporate workflow where you spin up temporary teams of AI bots and people to complete a single project and then delete them.
confusing: What on earth 'Agile' is supposed to mean in this context.
What 'agents' are, software bots, real estate agents, secret agents?
Why someone named Dinis Cruz suddenly appeared at the top of a family tree diagram.
Tech jargon like CRM, c.productions, and conductor.c that mean nothing to normal people.
answer.best_moment: The very first glowing jellyfish-like diagram before I realized it was an organizational chart.
answer.one_change: Delete the history lesson about corporate manifestos and actually show a tangible real-world thing being created instead of endless glowing org charts.
answer.weakest_moment: Scene 2, where the screen gets covered by a massive, boring wall of text about workplace processes.
answer.what_i_would_do_tomorrow: Swipe instantly to the next video, probably a funny cat clip or a recipe.

what_they_agree_on: All five would still stop; none would watch to the end, but three now stay to 17 to 28 seconds (v0.1: 7 to 18, one at 45).
The Manifesto page still loses the two viewers outside software (at 7 and 10 seconds).
All five ask for one concrete thing: a cell visibly making a real deliverable, then being taken down.
Two still read a 50-role chart as bureaucracy beside the first value; the film asserts the link and does not show it.
